intro: **Iodine** is essential for thyroid hormones (T3, T4) and fetal brain development. According to the **CDC** and the **NIH Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS)**, the US **RDA** is **150 mcg/day for adults**, rising to **220 mcg during pregnancy** and **290 mcg while breastfeeding** — the same thresholds endorsed by the **American Thyroid Association (ATA)** for US clinicians. Iodized table salt (FDA-permitted at 45 mcg per ¼ tsp) has been the main US dietary source since the 1920s, but mild deficiency has reappeared among Americans choosing **Himalayan pink, sea, or kosher salt** (typically not iodized) and those cutting sodium. This calculator returns your target intake by life stage and lists the best US food sources: iodized salt, seafood, dairy, and prenatal vitamins.

explanation:
## What is Iodine

A trace mineral essential for synthesizing thyroid hormones (T3 and T4), which regulate metabolism, body temperature, heart rate, and neurological development. The body cannot produce iodine — it must come entirely from diet or supplements.

## How This Calculator Works

Enter your life stage and weight. The calculator compares your estimated daily intake (from food sources you log) against the RDA established by the Institute of Medicine (IOM). It does **not** measure your actual iodine status — only a urinary iodine concentration (UIC) test can do that. Use this tool to identify dietary gaps, not to diagnose deficiency.

## Daily Recommended Intake (RDA)

| Life Stage | mcg/day |
|---|---|
| Infant 0–6 months | 110 (AI) |
| Infant 7–12 months | 130 (AI) |
| Children 1–8 years | 90 |
| Children 9–13 years | 120 |
| Adolescents/Adults | 150 |
| Pregnancy | 220 |
| Breastfeeding | 290 |

> **Note:** Values for infants are Adequate Intake (AI), not true RDAs, because data is insufficient to establish a precise requirement. Source: IOM, 2001.

## Why Pregnancy and Breastfeeding Need So Much More

The fetal thyroid gland doesn't become functional until week 10–12 of gestation, so the mother's iodine supply is the sole source of thyroid hormones for early fetal brain development. The WHO estimates iodine deficiency remains the **leading preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide**. Even mild-to-moderate deficiency during pregnancy — without overt symptoms in the mother — is associated with lower IQ scores in children (Lancet, 2013).

## Food Sources (mcg per 100g)

| Food | Iodine |
|---|---|
| Kelp seaweed | 2,000–40,000 ⚠️ |
| Nori (dried, 10g sheet) | ~35 |
| Cod | 170 |
| Iodized salt (1g) | 20–40 |
| Hake | 50 |
| Salmon | 40 |
| Dairy products | 40–80 |
| Egg (whole) | 25 |
| Yogurt | 30 |

**Why dairy varies so much:** Iodine content in milk depends heavily on whether cows were fed iodine-supplemented feed and whether iodophor sanitizers were used in milking equipment — not just the food itself. Organic dairy sometimes contains less iodine for this reason.

**Why seaweed is unpredictable:** Species and geographic origin produce extreme variation. A single gram of kombu can exceed the adult UL. Nori and wakame are far lower and generally safer for regular consumption.

## Iodized Salt Standards

Many countries mandate iodized salt to prevent deficiency. Argentina's Law 17,259 (1967) requires 15–40 mg of iodine per kg of table salt. The WHO recommends 20–40 mg/kg globally. **Critical caveat:** Iodine in salt degrades over time — salt stored in open containers, exposed to heat or humidity, can lose 50–75% of its iodine content within months. Store in sealed, opaque containers away from the stove.

Switching to non-iodized specialty salts (Himalayan, sea salt, kosher salt) without compensating through other sources is one of the most common causes of inadequate intake in developed countries.

## Iodine Deficiency Consequences

- **Pregnancy**: Fetal cognitive delay, irreversible cretinism (severe deficiency), subclinical IQ reduction (mild deficiency)
- **Adults**: Goiter (thyroid enlargement), hypothyroidism, fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance
- **Children**: Impaired cognitive development, poor school performance, growth retardation

Globally, ~2 billion people have insufficient iodine intake. Deficiency is not only a developing-world problem — populations using non-iodized salt, low-seafood diets, or living far from the sea are at risk anywhere.

## Excess Iodine and Upper Limits

- **Upper Limit (UL): 1,100 mcg/day** for adults (IOM)
- A single serving of kelp-based supplements can provide 500–3,000 mcg
- Chronic excess can paradoxically **inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis** (Wolff-Chaikoff effect)
- In genetically susceptible individuals, high iodine intake can trigger or worsen **Hashimoto's thyroiditis** (autoimmune hypothyroidism)
- Iodine-based contrast agents used in medical imaging can cause transient thyroid disruption — inform your doctor if you have thyroid disease

## What This Calculator Does NOT Include

- Iodine from medications (amiodarone contains ~37% iodine by weight)
- Iodine from drinking water (varies widely by region)
- Absorption differences caused by goitrogens (raw cruciferous vegetables like cabbage, cassava, and soy can mildly interfere with thyroid iodine uptake at very high intakes — clinically relevant mainly in pre-existing deficiency)
- Individual thyroid conditions that alter iodine requirements

## Common Mistakes

1. **Replacing iodized salt with pink or sea salt** without adjusting diet — these contain negligible iodine
2. **Vegans and plant-based diets**: No reliable plant sources except seaweed; supplementation is typically necessary
3. **Overconsumption of kelp or seaweed supplements** without checking iodine content per serving
4. **Prenatal vitamins without iodine**: Not all prenatal supplements include iodine — check the label; the American Thyroid Association recommends 150 mcg/day of supplemental iodine during pregnancy and breastfeeding
5. **Improper salt storage** that degrades iodine content before consumption

## Related Calculators

- **Selenium**: Works synergistically with iodine — selenoproteins are required to convert T4 to active T3; deficiency in both minerals amplifies thyroid dysfunction
- **Thyroid function overview**: Context for interpreting iodine needs in clinical conditions

faq.q: How much iodine do I need during pregnancy?
faq.a: 220 mcg/day according to WHO and NIH guidelines. For example, Argentina's Law 17,259 (1967) requires table salt to contain iodine (15–40 mg/kg).

faq.q: Does pink Himalayan salt contain iodine?
faq.a: No. Most non-iodized salts lack iodine, potentially causing deficiency.

faq.q: Is seaweed a good iodine source?
faq.a: Yes, in moderation. Kelp can be extremely high (2,000+ mcg/serving), so be cautious.
Most do—typically around 150 mcg. Check your label to confirm.

faq.q: Can too much iodine be harmful?
faq.a: Yes. The upper limit is 1,100 mcg/day. Excess iodine can trigger thyroiditis.

faq.q: How do vegans and vegetarians get enough iodine?
faq.a: Use iodized salt, consume moderate seaweed (like nori), or take a 150 mcg supplement.

faq.q: Can iodine deficiency affect my baby?
faq.a: Yes. Severe deficiency during pregnancy can cause intellectual disability and cretinism.

faq.q: What are the signs of iodine deficiency?
faq.a: Goiter (enlarged thyroid), fatigue, weight gain, difficulty concentrating, and cognitive issues.
